column5: remembering YHWH as prayer reaches the holy temple
column6: At the point of inner collapse, Jonah says that he remembered YHWH and that his prayer came to God in the holy temple. It is one of the Hebrew Bible's most exact remembered-Lord-to-prayer sequences.

column5: thanksgiving sacrifice, vowed act, and YHWH's salvation
column6: Jonah promises sacrifice with a voice of thanksgiving and fulfillment of his vow, then declares that salvation belongs to YHWH. This gives a distinctive prayerful completion to the commentary's purification, Name, worship, and salvation pattern.

column5: sign, zikkaron, and Torah in the mouth
column6: The exodus rite is to be a sign and zikkaron so that YHWH's Torah will be in Israel's mouth. Hebrew zikkaron belongs to the zkr cognate family of the commentary's ذ ك ر, and the verse explicitly joins memorial, embodied sign, and spoken teaching.

column5: write the memorial in a book and recite it
column6: YHWH orders Moses to write the event as a zikkaron in a book and place it in Joshua's ears. The zkr cognate supplies a concrete biblical precedent for the commentary's secondary sense of dhikr as a preserved, spoken scriptural record.

column5: seeing a sign, remembering commands, and doing them
column6: The tassel is to prompt Israel to remember all YHWH's commands and do them rather than follow heart and eyes astray. It provides a direct sequence from material reminder through remembrance to completed action.

column5: written song taught and put in Israel's mouth
column6: Moses is commanded to write the song, teach it to Israel, and put it in their mouths so it can remain a witness. The verse makes preserved words, oral repetition, and durable communal memory one practice.

column5: kneeling three times daily in prayer and thanksgiving
column6: Daniel kneels on his knees three times each day, prays, and gives thanks before God as was his custom. It is a sharply drawn biblical portrait of habitual bodily prayer joined to thankful remembrance.

column5: penitence, kneeling, and outspread hands to YHWH
column6: At the evening offering Ezra rises from fasting, falls on his knees, and spreads his hands to YHWH. The bodily action is expressly penitential, providing a close counterpart to purification culminating in prayer.

column5: fire and glory answered by prostration and thanks
column6: When Israel sees the fire and YHWH's glory, the people bow face-down and worship with thanksgiving. Unlike the commentary's opposed fire and prayer portraits, this temple scene makes divine fire the immediate occasion of worship.

column5: bowing and kneeling before the maker
column6: The summons is to worship, bow down, and kneel before YHWH the maker. Its Creator-language and successive bodily verbs make it a close poetic counterpart to the commentary's rabb as creator and prayer as embodied service.

column5: cup of salvation and calling YHWH's Name
column6: The psalmist lifts the cup of salvation and calls on YHWH's Name. It connects the salvation language surrounding 87:14 with a named, physical act of thanksgiving in 87:15.

column5: giving thanks and calling on YHWH's Name
column6: The liturgical charge joins thanksgiving, calling on YHWH's Name, and making his deeds known among peoples. It supplies a public vocal form of the Name-remembrance developed in the commentary.

column5: glory due the Name, offering, and worship
column6: The assembly is told to give YHWH the glory due his Name, bring an offering, and worship in holy splendor. It traces an explicit movement from the Name's honor to embodied cultic action.

column5: commanded praise becoming song and bowed worship
column6: Hezekiah directs Levites to praise YHWH with David's and Asaph's words; they praise with joy and bow to worship. The scene closely resembles the commentary's interest in an inherited command or text reaching fulfillment in human action.

column5: standing to bless the exalted glorious Name
column6: The Levites command the people to stand and bless YHWH, whose glorious Name is exalted above every blessing and praise. It directly supports the commentary's Name-as-elevated image while retaining a communal liturgical posture.

column5: prayer toward the house and confessing God's Name
column6: In drought, Israel prays toward the temple, confesses God's Name, and turns from sin. The verse brings together sanctuary, Name, prayer, repentance, and ethical correction more specifically than a general temple parallel.

column5: competing Name-invocation judged by fire
column6: Elijah contrasts calling on the name of a god with calling on YHWH, and identifies the God who answers by fire as God. The contest makes fire an authentication of correct Name-invocation, a distinct narrative arrangement beside the commentary's fire contrast.

column5: God sanctifies the great Name among nations
column6: God promises to vindicate the holiness of his great Name before the nations. It supplies a restoration-oracle counterpart to the commentary's insistence that the Name is exalted and not a neutral verbal label.

column5: clean water cleansing impurity and idols
column6: God promises to sprinkle clean water so that Israel will be clean from impurities and idols. It is a direct prophetic form of purification that prepares a people for restored relation to their Lord.

column5: new heart and new spirit
column6: God gives a new heart and spirit in place of the hardened one. This intensifies the commentary's inner dimension of remembrance by making transformed inward life part of restoration.

column5: Spirit causing God's statutes to be done
column6: God puts his Spirit within the restored people and causes them to walk in his statutes and do his judgments. It gives a strong biblical analogue for remembered or received divine speech becoming enacted human work.

column5: lips purified by the coal
column6: The seraph touches Isaiah's mouth with a coal and declares his guilt removed and sin atoned for. It gives a specific prophetic image of speech-organs purified before their subsequent service to the holy Lord.

column5: lips that honor while the heart is distant
column6: The people draw near with mouth and honor God with lips while their heart is far away. This is the Hebrew Bible's direct inverse of the commentary's united tongue-and-heart remembrance.

column5: purified lips calling the Name and serving together
column6: God gives peoples a purified lip so that all may call on YHWH's Name and serve him shoulder to shoulder. The verse unusually combines purified speech, Name-invocation, and communal embodied service.

column5: great Name among nations with incense and pure offering
column6: From sunrise to sunset YHWH's Name is great among nations, and incense and a pure offering are brought to it. This creates a global liturgical counterpart to the commentary's elevated Name and its movement from one worshipper to many places.

column5: not profaning and sanctifying the holy Name
column6: Israel must not profane YHWH's holy Name, for he is to be sanctified among them. It is a priestly biblical ground for treating the Name as an object of reverent, morally disciplined worship.

column5: continuing to pray for the people
column6: Samuel says that ceasing to pray for Israel would itself be sin, and pairs prayer with teaching the good and right way. It adds a continuing communal-intercession dimension to the commentary's secondary understanding of salāt as petition for another's good.

column5: saying Lord, Lord versus doing the Father's will
column6: Jesus denies that everyone who says Lord, Lord enters the kingdom, limiting it to the one who does the Father's will. This directly tests any reading in which naming the Lord is sufficient without the embodied, ethical action the commentary itself emphasizes.

column5: penitent bodily prayer for mercy
column6: The tax collector stands at a distance, will not raise his eyes, beats his breast, and asks God for mercy as a sinner. The scene makes inward humility, body, and penitential prayer a single act.

column5: Father, glorify your Name
column6: Jesus' spoken petition asks the Father to glorify the divine Name, and a heavenly voice answers it. It is a concentrated Johannine Name-prayer formula with the commentary's elevation motif.

column5: asking in Jesus' Name for the Father's glory
column6: Jesus promises to do what is asked in his Name so that the Father may be glorified in the Son. The verse creates a specifically Christian linkage of named petition, divine response, and glorification.

column5: making the Father's Name known and keeping his word
column6: Jesus says he has made the Father's Name known to those given him, and that they have kept the word. It closely connects disclosed Name, preserved teaching, and obedient human response.

column5: unspoken groanings in intercessory prayer
column6: The Spirit intercedes in human weakness with groanings that cannot be spoken. It offers a precise Christian counterpart to the commentary's claim that remembrance and prayer exceed audible language.

column5: bodies presented as living sacrifice and rational worship
column6: Believers are urged to present their bodies as a living, holy, pleasing sacrifice, called their worship. This makes the body itself the offered form of worship, a strong companion to the commentary's mouth-to-body movement.

column5: glorifying God in the body
column6: Those bought at a price are told to glorify God in their body. It gives an unusually compact New Testament statement that bodily life can enact the praise owed to God.

column5: praying and singing with spirit and mind
column6: Paul resolves to pray and sing both with spirit and with mind. The deliberately paired faculties make it a close comparison for the commentary's outward and inward registers of remembrance.

column5: spoken psalms and heart-song to the Lord
column6: Believers address one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs while singing and making melody in their hearts to the Lord. It joins communal voiced praise to interior devotion without collapsing either into the other.

column5: thanksgiving to the Father in Jesus' Name
column6: The community gives thanks always to God the Father in the Name of the Lord Jesus Christ. It provides a clear Christian formula in which named Lordship governs verbal worship.

column5: word dwelling within and gratitude sung to God
column6: The word of Christ is to dwell richly among believers through teaching, admonition, and grateful singing to God. It gives a churchly analogue to the commentary's dhikr as a preserved word active in heart, mouth, and communal practice.

column5: word and deed done in the Lord's Name
column6: Whatever believers do in word or deed is to be done in the Name of the Lord Jesus with thanksgiving to God. It makes the named Lord the bridge between speech and embodied action.

column5: remembering a person in petitions night and day
column6: Paul says he remembers Timothy unceasingly in his petitions night and day. The verse supplies a concrete Christian instance in which remembrance is itself maintained through ongoing prayer for another.

column5: loud cries, tears, reverence, and being heard
column6: Jesus offers prayers and supplications with loud cries and tears to the one able to save from death, and is heard because of reverence. This is a vivid counterweight to hidden prayer, showing the commentary's voice-and-body theme in an explicitly audible form.

column5: confession, prayer for one another, and healing
column6: Believers are told to confess sins and pray for each other so that they may be healed; the righteous person's prayer is powerful. It links purification, reciprocal petition, and beneficial effect in a single communal instruction.

column5: confession followed by forgiveness and cleansing
column6: Confession brings God's forgiveness and cleansing from all unrighteousness. The verse offers a tightly connected Christian account of voiced acknowledgement and divine purification.

column5: white garments and confession of the victor's name
column6: The victor is clothed in white, and Christ confesses that person's name before the Father and angels. It combines purification imagery, a personal name, and a reciprocal heavenly acknowledgement.

column5: fear God, give glory, and worship the creator
column6: The angelic proclamation calls all to fear God, give him glory, and worship the maker of heaven, earth, sea, and springs. Its Creator-centered worship and reverent fear echo major details developed around rabb and prayer.

column5: confession before the communal offering is made pure
column6: The Didache directs the assembly to confess transgressions before giving thanks and breaking bread, so that its sacrifice may be pure. It is an early Christian liturgical sequence of purification into worship.

column5: God no longer remembers forgiven sin
column6: In the new-covenant promise, God forgives iniquity and says he will remember sin no more. The negated Hebrew zkr verb gives a precise counter-form of remembrance: human dhikr preserves the Lord's Name, whereas divine mercy refuses to preserve forgiven guilt.

column5: atonement requires reconciliation with the injured person
column6: The Mishnah says that the Day of Atonement atones offenses against God but not offenses against another person until reconciliation is made. It sharpens the commentary's purification-and-prayer motif by making ethical repair indispensable.

column5: worship tied to neither mountain nor Jerusalem
column6: Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that worship of the Father will be tied neither to that mountain nor to Jerusalem. This is a specific Christian counter-reading beside the commentary's discussion of named worship houses and sacred places.

column5: true worship in spirit and truth
column6: The Father seeks worshippers who worship in spirit and truth. This develops the preceding relocation of worship into an inwardly truthful mode, useful beside the commentary's simultaneous concern for hidden remembrance and bodily rite.

column5: the appointed hour of prayer at the temple
column6: Peter and John go up to the temple at the hour of prayer. It offers an early Christian scene of continuing scheduled prayer within a named sacred space.

column5: fasting and prayer night and day in the temple
column6: Anna remains at the temple, worshipping through fasting and petitions night and day. This is a specific New Testament portrait of recurrent, bodily disciplined worship.

column5: communal worship and fasting followed by divine direction
column6: While the Antiochene community worships the Lord and fasts, the Holy Spirit gives a directive. The scene offers a concrete continuation of the commentary's reminder-to-action pattern within communal liturgy.

column5: things sanctified through God's word and prayer
column6: A created thing is said to be sanctified through God's word and prayer. It provides a distinct Christian use of prayer as a consecrating act, rather than simply as petition or praise.

column5: acceptable worship with reverence and awe
column6: Recipients of the unshakable kingdom are urged to offer worship pleasing to God with reverence and awe. It closely matches the commentary's fearful recipient of reminder and its account of worship as the proper response.
